answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (child resources include databases, collections etc.).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (part of core az CLI). Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=uksouth --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (with appropriate apiVersion). Terraform (azurerm provider): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "..." resource_group_name = "..." offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer:
Typical MongoDB-compatible connection string for Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB MongoDB API):
mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin&retryWrites=false
You can also see an SRV form: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin
Notes: host suffix is *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com, TLS port is 10255, required options include TLS/ssl=true (or tls=true), often replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false; authSource=admin is commonly required for Cosmos-mapped users.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB) uses Request Units (RUs) for provisioned throughput and also offers a serverless option. Typical billing is RU/s for provisioned throughput or pay-per-request in serverless. (Example CLI to set throughput: az cosmosdb sql database throughput update --resource-group RG --account-name myAccount --name myDb --throughput 400). It does not use the MongoDB Atlas-style vCore instance classes for the Cosmos DB MongoDB API.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API you authenticate with standard MongoDB credentials (username/password created on the Cosmos account) or the account's primary/master keys exposed as Mongo credentials. Resource tokens (for fine grained access) are also used in Cosmos DB generally. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) token-based authentication is not supported by the MongoDB wire-protocol drivers for Cosmos DB; AAD-based auth is supported for some Cosmos DB APIs (SQL) using Azure AD tokens, but not for the MongoDB API. So in practice the Node mongodb driver uses the username/password from the account's connection string.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (for Node.js use the official mongodb npm package). There is not a separate MongoDB-specific Azure SDK for application data-plane access; the Azure SDKs (e.g., @azure/cosmos) are for the Core/SQL API. For a MongoDB-compatible account use the normal mongodb driver and point it at the cosmos account URI.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: For simple full-text you can use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ textField: "text" })). For richer full-text/hybrid search (text + vectors) integrate Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search (index Cosmos data in Azure Cognitive Search) or export documents to a search engine. If the managed service offers built-in vector indexes, combine a Mongo text index with the vector index and do hybrid scoring client-side (text filter/sort via Mongo, vector nearest-neighbor via vector index endpoint) or use an external hybrid search engine.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Compatibility depends on the account configuration; recent Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB MongoDB API) supports modern MongoDB wire protocol versions (examples up to MongoDB 6.0+; newer clusters may advertise 7.0). Common unsupported or partial features: server-side JavaScript (db.eval, $where), certain admin and diagnostic commands, some storage-engine-specific features, and some edge-case aggregation operators/extensions. Expect differences in transaction semantics and in behavior of certain admin or performance knobs. Always verify the supported MongoDB server version for your account in the portal/CLI.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for SQL API (Windows/Linux container), but it historically does not fully emulate the MongoDB API. For MongoDB-compatible development use the official MongoDB server image locally: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:7 --bind_ip_all and connect on mongodb://localhost:27017. Use the real cloud account for features that the emulator doesn't support (vectors, provider-specific extensions).

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams (the MongoDB watch() API) are supported on MongoDB-compatible Cosmos accounts that advertise a supported MongoDB version. In most cases you can call collection.watch() from the driver; if using Cosmos DB you may need an account version that supports change streams (verify account compatibility). For Cosmos DB there is also the native 'Change Feed' feature (separate, available for Core/SQL); for MongoDB API use watch() when the account supports it.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: The service-specific MCP server is 'documentdb' (the sample refers to the documentdb MCP server). Use the documentdb server/tooling/profile to inspect collections, indexes and query plans against the Mongo-compatible endpoint. The general Azure MCP Server (which covers ARM management) does not replace the documentdb agent for data-plane MongoDB inspection tools.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally shipped a service called DocumentDB (the document database engine that powered the SQL API). That product was rebranded and expanded into Azure Cosmos DB (multi‑API, globally distributed DB). 'DocumentDB' in Microsoft docs historically refers to the SQL API; Azure Cosmos DB also exposes a MongoDB-compatible API. The open-source 'DocumentDB' projects are unrelated; Microsoft’s DocumentDB was a proprietary predecessor to Cosmos DB.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath the MongoDB API is Cosmos DB's proprietary engine implementing the MongoDB wire protocol (a compatibility layer rather than a vanilla mongod). Application code should use standard MongoDB drivers, but expect behavioral differences (indexing semantics, RU consumption, query planner differences, unsupported admin commands, and different consistency/transaction guarantees). Test queries and index choices against the actual account.

answers.question: What exact database and collection names will this sample use and create?
answers.answer: Database: sample_fintech_02. Collections: transactions (stores transaction docs), embeddings (optional: stores vector embeddings if separated). All sample data and indexes go into sample_fintech_02 only.

answers.question: What index definitions does this sample need for transaction categorization and the aggregation endpoint?
answers.answer: Create a text index on the free-text fields used for categorization (e.g., db.transactions.createIndex({ description: 'text', merchant: 'text' })). Create a compound index for aggregation by category and date: db.transactions.createIndex({ category: 1, transactionDate: 1 }). If using vector search for semantic matching, create a vector index on the embedding field (example): db.transactions.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { vector: { dimensions: 1536, algorithm: 'hnsw', distanceMetric: 'cosine' } }).

answers.question: Exactly how will the Node.js app connect at runtime (command/driver syntax and environment variable)?
What validation/schema or sample documents will the sample write when creating test data?
answers.answer:
Each transaction doc shape the app will write: {
  _id: ObjectId,
  amount: Number,
  currency: 'USD'|'EUR'|..., 
  description: String,
  merchant: String,
  transactionDate: ISODate,
  category: null | String,       // assigned by the agent
  embedding: [Number],          // optional 1536-d vector produced by encoder
  source: 'bank'|'card'|'import'
}
The sample loader will insert a few dozen realistic transactions with category:null for the agent to classify.

answers.question: What prompt engineering and flow will the agent use to categorize a transaction and persist the result?
answers.answer:
Flow:
1) Query uncategorized transactions: db.transactions.find({ category: null }).limit(50)
2) For each transaction build a prompt that includes a fixed taxonomy and examples, e.g.:
   "Taxonomy: [Groceries, Dining, Utilities, Rent, Travel, Entertainment, Income, Transfer, Other].
    Examples:
    - 'WholeFoods purchase $23' => Groceries
    - 'Uber ride to airport' => Travel
    Now categorize this transaction:
    Description: '<description>'
    Merchant: '<merchant>'
    Amount: '<amount>'
    Date: '<transactionDate>'
    Respond with a single category from the taxonomy and an optional confidence number."
3) Send prompt to LLM via LangChain, parse single-category response.
4) Persist: db.transactions.updateOne({ _id: ... }, { $set: { category: '<Category>', categoryAssignedAt: new Date(), categoryConfidence: 0.92 } })
5) Expose an aggregation endpoint (e.g., /reports/monthly) that runs: db.transactions.aggregate([ { $match: { transactionDate: { $gte: start, $lt: end } } }, { $group: { _id: '$category', total: { $sum: '$amount' } } } ]) and returns monthly spend by category.
